source.title: On Anytime Learning at Macroscale
source.authors: Lucas Caccia; Jing Xu; Myle Ott; M. Ranzato; Ludovic Denoyer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study cites Kaplan et al. and reports model-size and training-regime results, but it does not test power-law loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model perplexity across model sizes and compute, but does not fit or assess power laws or test predictions from smaller runs. Its image-classification results report error rates rather than power-law loss. The language-model comparison of sequential and i.i.d. training is recorded as a related finding, not as a test of a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks sequential mega-batch training (ALMA) strategies. It reports perplexity and error rates across a few model sizes and expert counts but fits no power laws. It tests no extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape-at-fixed-parameters or downstream predictability. Its remark that larger models are more sample-efficient echoes Kaplan et al. qualitatively, but it is not a test of any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusions are broader than the record states. An intermediate waiting time is often best and greedy updating is not always optimal. Ensembles strike the best trade-off. Growing architectures do not beat fixed large models. Larger models are more statistically efficient. Sequential training is harder than i.i.d., more so for larger models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies sequential mega-batch learning and reports perplexity comparisons; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurements or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The sequential-versus-i.i.d. perplexity gap differs by model size and by the number of mega-batches (k=3 versus k=4).

fits_no_version.finding: For 2-component, 4-expert ensembles, sequential mega-batch training gave higher perplexity than i.i.d. training with equal data and compute. The gap was about 0.2-0.3 PPL for the small model and about 1.0-1.1 PPL for the big model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sequential multi-pass training over mega-batches harms LM perplexity relative to i.i.d. training, more so for larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models were more sample-efficient in CIFAR-10, MNIST and Switch-Transformer LM experiments. The large LM after one mega-batch beat all base models after four. This is a qualitative claim, with no power-law fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models reach a given error with less data across CNN, MLP and transformer models in streaming settings.

record.peer_reviewed: CoLLAs (1st Conference on Lifelong Learning Agents, published 2022)
record.problems: The language-model study uses four mega-batches and two model sizes; uncertainty estimates are not reported for the Table 1 comparisons. The paper does not fit power laws or test extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also presents broader language-model perplexity comparisons across model sizes, expert counts, methods, and training stages in Figure 5 and Appendix D, but does not report power-law fits or extrapolation tests; these were not extracted as tests of the listed versions.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss vs parameters, tokens or compute. Only two LM backbone sizes and four mega-batches.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
CNN/MLP error rates vs size and sequential training are reported, but no power-law form is assessed.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation and tranche (cites_only, T6) are confirmed. Kaplan et al. is cited only to say statistical efficiency of large models extends beyond transformers. The Table 2 and Figure 5 perplexity-vs-size data were reasonably left out, since no scaling form is assessed.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or assessment over several orders of magnitude; no separation of parameter, token, and compute effects.
No small-run fits or large-run loss predictions.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation analysis or fitted growth exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies image classification and sequential language-model training, but does not test whether power-law forms hold in these settings.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, and no test of curves bending away from a power law.
